overview: Businesses and groups sometimes lease buildings or land inside national parks, for example to run a lodge or restore a historic property. Under current rules, the National Park Service generally has to open a lease to competitive bidding when it ends. This bill lets the Interior Secretary extend a lease without bidding if the tenant has held it for at least five years, is following its terms and the extension serves the park, but only after publishing a 60-day notice inviting other interested operators; if a competitor offers better terms, the lease must go to bidding instead. Extensions longer than 10 years must be sent to Congress 30 days in advance, and the Park Service must review the tenant's compliance halfway through, with the option to end the lease if the tenant falls short. The bill also allows leases of up to 99 years for redevelopment projects expected to cost more than $100 million, with 60 days' notice to Congress for any lease over 60 years. As of October 5, 2026, it had passed the Senate and was waiting for action in the House.
for: Supporters say longer, more predictable leases give tenants a reason to invest heavily in repairing aging park buildings, which saves the Park Service money while keeping safeguards like public notice and compliance reviews.
against: Critics say letting leases be extended without bidding, or locked in for up to 99 years, weakens competition and could tie up public park property with a single private operator for generations.
